edges.effect_quant: A 2010 review of remission-maintenance studies reported that Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG alone or with mesalazine showed a nonsignificant decrease in relapse odds but a longer time to relapse than mesalazine alone. Supportive findings also come from a 117-patient cohort in post-surgical ulcerative colitis showing delayed first pouchitis with LGG, but broader systematic review evidence for ulcerative colitis remains limited and strain-specific.
edges.population: adults with inactive ulcerative colitis or ulcerative colitis after ileal pouch-anal anastomosis exposed to Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG-based probiotic therapy
edges.mechanism: Lactobacillus rhamnosus may help maintain remission by supporting mucosal barrier function and shifting inflammatory signaling at the host-microbe interface, but the effect appears highly strain- and context-specific. The modest and indirect human evidence suggests it may extend relapse-free time in some settings without establishing a robust universal remission-maintenance effect.
edges.summary: Lactobacillus rhamnosus has mixed and limited evidence for maintaining ulcerative colitis remission. Some data suggest a longer relapse-free interval or downstream benefit in pouch-related disease after ulcerative colitis surgery, but the direct remission signal is not strong enough to treat this as an established maintenance therapy.
edges.caveats: This edge leans heavily on strain-specific LGG data and includes pouchitis prevention after ulcerative colitis surgery, which is related but not identical to quiescent luminal UC remission. The evidence base is too sparse and heterogeneous to support a firm positive claim.

evidence.notes: Probiotics for maintaining remission of ulcerative colitis in adults.

evidence.citation: Zocco et al 2004 Dis Colon Rectum
evidence.notes: Delay of the first onset of pouchitis by oral intake of the probiotic strain Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG.
